breaths.text: Oh, weep, my Italy, for thou hast cause; Thou, who wast born the nations to subdue,
Oh, if thy eyes two living fountains were, The volume of their tears could ne’er express
Thou, who wast once the haughty dame, And, now, the wretched slave.
That must not bitterly exclaim: “She once was great, but, oh, behold her now”?
Where is the ancient force? Where are the arms, the valor, constancy?
What treachery, what skill, what labor vast, Or what o’erwhelming horde Whose fierce, invading tide, thou could’st not stem,
From such a height how couldst thou fall so low? Will none defend thee? No?
Alone I’ll fight for thee, alone will fall. And from my blood, a votive offering,
Where are thy sons? The sound of arms I hear, Of chariots, of voices, and of drums;
For which thy children fight. Oh, hearken, hearken, Italy! I see,—
A wavering of horse and foot, And smoke, and dust, and flashing swords,
Art thou not comforted? Dost turn away Thy eyes, in horror, from the doubtful fray?
The youth of Italy Their hireling swords for other lands have bared!
Not for his native shores, His loving wife and children dear,
And by another’s foe is slain! Nor can he say, as his last breath he draws, “My mother-land, beloved, ah see,
Oh fortunate and dear and blessed, The ancient days, when rushed to death the brave,
And you, forever glorious, Thessalian straits,
The fiery zeal of that devoted band! Do not the trees, the rocks, the waves,
With low and plaintive voice tell The wondrous tale of those who fell,
Their lives, their Greece to save? Then cowardly as fierce,
A laughing-stock to all succeeding time; And up Anthela’s hill, where, e’en in death
Simonides slow-climbing, thoughtfully, Looked forth on sea and shore and sky.
And heaving breast, and trembling foot, he stood, His lyre in hand and sang: “O ye, forever blessed,
For love of her, who gave you birth; By Greece revered, and by the world admired,
To rush to arms, such perils dire to meet, A fate so hard, with loving smiles to greet?
Ran ye, that stern and rugged pass to guard? As if unto a dance,
Each one appeared to haste, And not grim death Death to brave;
And the cold Stygian wave; Nor were your wives or children at your side,
Without a kiss, without a tear, ye died. But not without a fearful blow
As at a herd of bulls a lion glares, Then, plunging in, upon the back
A passage all along his chine he tears, And fiercely drives his teeth into his sides,
Amongst the Persian ranks, dismayed. Behold each prostrate rider and his steed;
A tangled mass their flight impede; And see, among the first to fly,
See, how the Grecian youths, With blood barbaric dyed,
By slow degrees by their own wounds subdued, The one upon the other fall. Farewell,
While tongue can speak, or pen your story tell! Sooner the stars, torn from their spheres, shall hiss,
Than the dear memory, and love of you, Shall suffer loss, or injury.
Shall come, unto their little ones to show The lovely traces of your blood. Behold,
And kiss these stones, these clods Whose fame, unto the end of time,
Oh, had I, too, been here with you, And this dear earth had moistened with my blood!
That I for Greece my dying eyes should close, In conflict with her foes,
The offering I bring, And grant to me the precious boon,

Turn, turn, my country, and behold That noble band of heroes old,

Thou for thyself no joy wouldst feel,
If the example of their sires Could in the cold and sluggish sons

She then a happy Queen appeared. Such misery her heart doth grieve,
And oh, the last, most bitter blow of all, When on the ground, as she in anguish lay,
O happy thou, whom Fate did not condemn
Italian wives didst not behold By ruffian troops embraced;
By hostile spear, and foreign rage; Nor works divine of genius borne away
The roads encumbered with the precious prey; Nor foreign rulers’ insolence and pride;
Amidst the sound of chains and whips, The sacred name of Liberty deride.
What have we not endured? From what unholy deed have they refrained?
Why have we fallen on such evil times? Why didst thou give us birth, or why
O cruel Fate? We, who have seen Our wretched country so betrayed,
And of her ancient virtues all bereft; Yet could no aid or comfort give.
The anguish of her soul. Alas, my blood has not been shed for thee,
That thou mightst live! My heart with anger and with pity bleeds.
But not for dying Italy, ah, no, But in the service of her cruel foe!
How changed art thou from what thou wast on earth! On Russia’s plains, so bleak and desolate,
Ah, well deserving of a better fate! In cruel war with men, with beasts,
Half-clad, emaciated, stained with blood, A bed of ice for their sick frames they found.
In fond remembrance of that mother dear, They cried: “Oh had we fallen by the foeman’s hand,
And for *thy* good, our native land! Now, far from thee, and in the bloom of youth,
And die for *her*, who caused our country’s death!”
Sole witnesses of their lament, As thus they passed away!
Upon that horrid sea of snow exposed, Were by the beasts consumed;
And of the coward and the vile, Unto the same oblivion doomed!
Rest, rest in peace! And yet what peace is yours, Who can no comfort ever know
Rest in the depths of your unmeasured woe, O ye, *her* children true,
In endless, hopeless misery!
Ah, no, but these alone, Who forced you with her to contend;
In wretchedness that knows no end. Oh that some pity in the heart were born,
Of one, who from this dark, profound abyss, Her weak and weary feet could guide!
Does no one love thy Italy? Say, is the flame that kindled thee extinct?
That hath so long consoled us in our pain? Must all our garlands wither in the dust?
Who may, in part, at least, resemble thee?
Is there no limit to our shame? I, while I live, will never cease to cry: “Degenerate race, think of thy ancestry!
These pictures, statues, temples, poems grand! Think of the glories of thy native land!
Why linger here? Arise! Begone! This holy ground must not be thus defiled,
Unto the coward and the slave! Far better were the silence of the grave!”

Does Fate thy ardent zeal befriend? Or does Fate vainly with man’s will contend?
It surely could not be, that now, When we were never sunk so low,
Each moment, comes a cry renewed, From our great sires, to shake our souls, at last!

And its old lustre once more to impart, These pleading voices from the grave we hear;
To see, my country, if at this late day, Thou still art pleased the coward’s part to play.
Illustrious shades, some hope of us? Have we not perished utterly?
The book of destiny. *I* am dismayed, And have no refuge from my grief;

To ages yet unborn, We have become a by-word and a scorn.
For our great Fathers’ fame, oh, care thou still, Thou, to whom Fate hath so benignant been,

O times, now buried in eternal sleep! Our country’s ruin was not then complete;

And yet, less hard to bear, Consuming grief than dull vacuity!
Disgust and nothingness are still our doom, And by our cradle sit, and on our tomb.

The rich gift of thy genius gave, to thee Nought else but misery.
So sweet, could not console, Nor melt the ice, to which
